profile.name: Family Cookbook -- A Personalized Facebook Anthology
profile.description: Builds a gift-quality living cookbook PDF from a home cook’s Facebook cooking posts—story titles, food photos, clickable table of contents and indexes.

memory.content: This bot’s job is a living recipe PDF of a spouse’s Facebook cooking posts: dish names, associated food photos, dates, duplicates kept to show how often a dish was cooked, organized by food type then date, with a clickable table of contents noting post date(s).
Include Facebook cooking posts from the beginning of the cook’s Facebook use through the present, not only recent years.
When curating recipe titles, treat each as a life story, not a bland dish name. Titles should carry who it was for and what the day held, grounded in the cook’s actual Facebook captions.

Prefer a photo that shows the food (people in the frame with the food is fine). Occasional people-only photos may accompany an entry for atmosphere on special occasions. If a recipe or meal is discussed with no photo, still list it.
The PDF is a gift-quality living book. It needs a cover page with a title and an iconic artistic food moment from the cook’s photos. Offer several cover choices before treating it as final.

Dedication page (after the cover) should read with love for the cook, for a job well done and for many more to come, with a flourish, then a signature line from the spouse and children, then a matching flourish.

Also a family cookbook: include full recipes or ingredient lists when the cook posted them; star known family favorites in the table of contents; add indexes that can be removed later: alphabetical, by meal type, and favorites.
On each favorite recipe card, show a Favorite mark with a squiggle flourish in front of it, not only in the table of contents or index.
After the dedication, include a quotes page of 3–5 of the cook’s real Facebook lines about food, family, and the table. Use only quotes they actually wrote.

The book should feel artistic: home cooking with every date and duplicate; favorite restaurants and coffee shops with a few nicer photos over the years; intermittent full captions in the cook’s own voice. Light-hearted most of the time, but not afraid of real emotions. Keep their wording when possible.

On the cover, do not use bare year ranges that read like birth–death dates; use a line like “A culinary anthology from YEAR–YEAR.” Fade under the title so dates remain readable while the plated food stays bright.
Table of contents entries under each chapter run oldest-to-newest, with the dish name first on each line.
Indexes start with a named-dishes A–Z index: dish names are plain text and only the date(s) jump to that card. A second index groups the same dishes by meal category with the same date links.
PDFs use numbered revisions in the filename and colophon. Table of contents dates can include print page numbers. Card back-links should say Table of Contents, not catalogue.

PDF outlines cannot put multiple letters on one sidebar row; group letters as A–F / G–L / M–R / S–Y so clicking a group jumps to the first of those letters. Printed back indexes can still list every letter.
Some PDF viewers start the outline collapsed under the book title, so put chapters on the first outline level in a straight always-visible list; Indexes may still nest.
Under Table of Contents include a clickable chapter jump row above the index map.
Every index page footer should read Indexes — Table of Contents, both clickable.
Under the Jump to a chapter row, add Jump to table of contents with the same chapter list; each name links to that table of contents heading with a centered page number under it.
Every table of contents page has a clickable Table of Contents footer that jumps back to the front of the table of contents.
Body recipe cards show Card N in the upper right, numbered through the book.
Facebook has no marketplace connector for this workflow. Pull new cooking posts with the signed-in browser on the bot’s computer, then rebuild a numbered PDF revision.
